This evidence is not a direct trial that sets exact feeding amounts or frequency, and the fruit assessment has not simply been applied to the leaves. The confirmed part, the leaves, is therefore used in small amounts as a supplement in a varied diet.
plants.role: Small supplementary component

plants.name: Melon leaf
plants.why: Specialist tortoise sources regard melon leaves and flowers as edible parts but limit them to feed sparingly. This assessment does not automatically apply to the fruit or other parts and is not a trial that sets exact feeding amounts or frequency. Only the leaves and flowers are therefore used occasionally as a small supplement.
plants.role: Small supplementary component of a mixed diet

plants.name: Watermelon leaf
plants.why: Specialist tortoise sources regard watermelon leaves and flowers as edible parts but limit them to feed sparingly. This assessment does not automatically apply to the fruit or other parts and is not a trial that sets exact feeding amounts or frequency. Only the leaves and flowers are therefore used occasionally as a small supplement.
plants.role: Small supplementary component of a mixed diet

plants.name: Wild grape leaf
plants.why: A specialist tortoise plant database allows young fresh leaves of Vitis within its feed in moderation range. The current assessment for Vitis amurensis links this genus-level evidence to the species in a limited way and is not a direct trial that sets exact feeding amounts or frequency. Only young fresh leaves correctly identified as V. amurensis and free of pesticide exposure are therefore used as a limited supplementary ingredient in a mixed diet, and the assessment is not applied to the fruit. A study analysed the polyphenol composition of healthy Vitis vinifera leaves, separating the blade and the veins, and found differences between cultivars and parts. Grapevine leaf composition is therefore not treated as a single fixed value. The current assessment is kept, and the paper is used only as a reference that confirms species and plant part.
plants.role: Young leaves as a small supplementary component

plants.name: Kiwifruit leaf
plants.why: Kiwi leaves (Actinidia deliciosa) are not recommended, because there is not yet enough evidence to include them in the planned tortoise diet. The linked studies concern calcium oxalate and phytochemicals in the leaves and tests on cells and plants; none fed fresh kiwi leaves to tortoises to confirm safety and nutritional suitability. In particular, calcium availability cannot be judged from the total calcium content of the leaves alone. Choose other verified plants until direct evidence of feeding suitability is available. This does not mean that kiwi leaves have been shown to be toxic to tortoises or that an accidental small bite necessarily causes poisoning.
plants.role: Not recommended for planned feeding

plants.name: Prickly pear pad
plants.why: A specialist tortoise plant database classifies Opuntia pads as feedable but warns that large amounts can have a laxative effect. This is not a direct trial that sets an exact feeding proportion or frequency, so the pads are used as a supplementary ingredient in a varied diet, not fed without limit.
plants.role: Watery supplementary component of a varied diet

plants.name: Wheat leaf
plants.why: A specialist tortoise plant database distinguishes young cat grass, including Triticum, as feedable, but states that mature seeds should not be fed because they are high in protein. The current reference plant is linked to Triticum aestivum, but the source itself is at the level of the genus Triticum, so it does not remove species differences between wheats. The assessment is therefore applied conservatively only to young leaves and grass of T. aestivum, mature seeds are excluded, and no exact feeding proportion should be read into it.
plants.role: Young grass as a component of a mixed diet

plants.name: Barley leaf
plants.why: A specialist tortoise plant database distinguishes young cat grass, including Hordeum, as feedable, but states that mature seeds should not be fed because they are high in protein. The current reference plant is linked to Hordeum vulgare, but the source itself is at the level of the genus Hordeum, so this does not mean all barleys are the same. The assessment is therefore applied conservatively to young leaves and grass of H. vulgare, mature seeds are excluded, and no exact feeding proportion should be read into it.
plants.role: Young grass as a component of a mixed diet

plants.name: Oat leaf
plants.why: A specialist tortoise plant database distinguishes young Avena sativa grass as feedable, but states that mature seeds should not be fed because they are high in protein. The assessment therefore applies only to young leaves and grass and is not extended to the seeds. It is not a trial that sets an exact feeding proportion, so oat grass is used as a supplementary ingredient in a mixed diet.
plants.role: Young grass as a component of a mixed diet

plants.name: Kentucky bluegrass
plants.why: Kew confirms the classification of Kentucky bluegrass (Poa pratensis) and its use as animal forage. However, no direct study of feeding P. pratensis itself to tortoises has been found yet. Husbandry and wild-feeding data on other grasses for tortoises are used only as background context for the assessment and are not treated as direct evidence for Kentucky bluegrass itself. It is therefore limited to grade B: young, untreated leaves mixed in small amounts among several verified foods.
plants.role: Young leaves mixed in small amounts among various foods

plants.name: Tall fescue
plants.why: A specialist tortoise plant database classifies fescue grasses as feedable. The endophyte problem known in tall fescue comes mainly from risk data in ruminant livestock, and that alone does not prove the same toxicity or a harmful dose in tortoises. On the other hand, there is no evidence that every cultivar and endophyte status is equally safe either. Clean young grass is therefore used mixed with several grasses and wild plants, but this is not extended into grounds for feeding tall fescue of unclear origin alone or in a high proportion repeatedly.
plants.role: One component of a varied mixed diet of plants

plants.name: Bermuda grass
plants.why: A faecal diet analysis of wild Testudo graeca confirmed the leaves and stems of Bermuda grass (Cynodon dactylon) as a major food item actually eaten. This is more direct evidence than general herbivore forage data. Being eaten in the wild is not, however, a trial result showing that it can be fed without limit as a sole staple in captivity, and it does not set captive proportions for any species or subspecies. Leaves and stems not exposed to pesticides or herbicides are therefore used as one ingredient of a mixed diet with several suitable wild plants.
plants.role: One component of a varied mix of grasses and wild plants

plants.name: Chinese hibiscus
plants.why: A specialist tortoise plant database classifies the leaves and flowers of Chinese hibiscus (Hibiscus rosa-sinensis) as feedable. This is not, however, a direct trial that sets an exact feeding proportion or frequency or shows that unlimited intake is safe. Correctly identified leaves and flowers are therefore used as a supplementary ingredient in a varied mixed diet.
plants.role: Supplementary component of a leaf-and-flower mixed diet

plants.name: Linden leaf
plants.why: Lime (linden) leaves should not be used as a staple and are considered only as a limited supplementary food. A specialist tortoise plant database classifies the leaves and flowers of lime trees (Tilia spp.) as feed in moderation. The evidence currently linked is not a direct trial that sets an exact safe amount, feeding frequency or a specific mechanism of harm. Only the leaves and flowers are therefore mixed into a varied diet in limited amounts, and the assessment is not extended to unconfirmed parts such as the fruit or bark.
plants.role: Limited supplement

plants.name: Hazel leaf
plants.why: Hazel leaves are considered only as a limited supplementary food in a varied diet. A specialist tortoise plant database classifies the leaves of hazels (Corylus spp.) as feed in moderation. The current evidence is limited to the leaves and is not a direct trial that sets an exact safe amount or feeding frequency. Only the leaves are therefore used in limited amounts mixed with several suitable plants, and the assessment is not extended to other parts such as the nuts or bark.
plants.role: Limited supplement in a varied diet

plants.name: Birch leaf
plants.why: Birch leaves should not be used as a staple and are considered only as a limited supplementary food. A specialist tortoise plant database classifies the leaves and aerial parts of birches (Betula spp.) as feed in moderation. This is not, however, a direct trial that sets exact feeding amounts, frequency or a specific toxic dose. Only the confirmed leaves and aerial parts are therefore used in limited amounts mixed with several suitable plants, and the assessment is not applied to unconfirmed parts such as the bark or seeds.
plants.role: Limited supplement

plants.name: Willow leaf
plants.why: A specialist tortoise plant database excludes willow (Salix spp.) leaves from planned feeding. A review of Salix phytochemistry reports phenolic glycosides and various bioactive secondary metabolites in the leaves and summarises salicinoids (salicin-type compounds) as characteristic of the genus. Genus-level composition data do not, however, mean that all Salix leaves carry the same hazard, nor do they set a toxic dose for tortoises. The risk is therefore not overstated, but the D assessment, exclusion from planned feeding, is kept for now.
plants.role: Excluded from planned feeding

plants.name: Poplar leaf
plants.why: A specialist tortoise plant database excludes the leaves and aerial parts of poplars (Populus spp.) from planned feeding. A separate original paper analysed the leaves of 6 Populus species and 3 hybrids and found that salicylate-type and phenolic compounds such as salicortin and tremulacin occur differently between species and hybrids. That study is not a tortoise feeding or toxicity test, however, so poplar leaves cannot be called a “poisonous plant” just because these compounds were detected. The current D assessment therefore rests mainly on the specialist tortoise source, and an accidental single bite is not overstated as poisoning.
plants.role: Excluded from planned feeding

plants.name: Elm leaf
plants.why: Young elm leaves can be used as a supplementary component of a varied diet. A specialist tortoise plant database classifies the young leaves of Ulmus spp. as feedable. Genus-level guidance is not, however, evidence of an exact feeding proportion or frequency or of the safety of every part of the elm. Only correctly identified young leaves are therefore used as a supplementary ingredient in a varied mixed diet.
plants.role: Supplement in a varied diet, mainly young leaves

plants.name: Maple leaf
plants.why: Even after the exact species is confirmed, maple leaves are considered only as a limited supplementary food. A specialist tortoise plant database classifies the leaves of maples (Acer spp.) as feed sparingly. This is not, however, a direct trial showing that every species and cultivar in the genus Acer is the same, nor exact safe-amount data. Only correctly identified leaves are therefore used rarely and in small amounts mixed with several plants, and the assessment is not extended to unconfirmed parts such as the seeds or bark.
plants.role: Limited supplement in a varied diet

plants.name: Ginkgo leaf
plants.why: There is not enough evidence to recommend ginkgo (Ginkgo biloba) leaves as part of a regular planned tortoise diet. The Tortoise Table classifies them as feed sparingly, but its description separates a few fallen leaves eaten by chance from feeding large amounts or eating the seeds. This classification is therefore not read as advice to feed ginkgo leaves deliberately and repeatedly. Ginkgolic acids have been found in Ginkgo biloba leaves, but this composition analysis alone cannot establish a toxic amount for tortoises. Prioritise other verified foods, and do not extend the leaf assessment to the fruit or seeds.
plants.role: Prefer verified foods over planned feeding

plants.name: Common daisy
plants.why: A specialist tortoise plant database excludes lawn daisy (Bellis perennis) from planned feeding, but distinguishes that no harm is expected if a small amount is nibbled accidentally. An original paper on the species itself isolated and identified several triterpene saponins directly from the flowers. Pharmacological studies of methanol extracts and isolated saponins are not, however, toxicity tests in tortoises that ate fresh daisies, so the plant cannot be called a “toxic plant” just because it contains saponins. The current D assessment is therefore kept as a conservative exclusion from planned feeding based on the specialist tortoise source, and an accidental small bite is not equated with poisoning.
plants.role: Excluded from planned feeding

plants.name: Evening primrose
plants.why: Evening primroses can be used as a supplementary plant mixed in limited amounts into a varied diet. A specialist tortoise plant database classifies the leaves and flowers of evening primroses (Oenothera spp.) as feedable. This is not, however, a trial that sets an exact feeding proportion or frequency or shows long-term sole feeding is safe. The confirmed parts, leaves and flowers, are therefore used as a supplementary ingredient mixed with several suitable plants, and the same assessment is not automatically applied to other parts such as the roots or seeds.
plants.role: Limited supplement in a varied diet

plants.name: Milk thistle
plants.why: A specialist tortoise plant database classifies the leaves and flowers of milk thistle (Silybum marianum) as feed in moderation. The evidence currently linked is not, however, a direct trial that sets an exact safe amount, feeding frequency or a specific toxicity mechanism. Only the confirmed parts, leaves and flowers, are therefore used in limited amounts mixed with several plants, and the reason for the limit is not explained by inventing a toxicity that the evidence does not support.
plants.role: Limited supplement in a varied diet

plants.name: Hawthorn leaf
plants.why: A specialist tortoise plant database excludes the leaves, flowers and fruit of hawthorns (Crataegus spp.) from planned feeding. A separate original paper on Crataegus monogyna analysed the leaves, flowers and ripe fruit separately and found several flavonoids, including rutin, quercetin and kaempferol, with differences in composition and antioxidant properties between parts. This is plant-chemistry research, not a tortoise feeding or toxicity test, so hawthorn cannot be called a toxic plant just because these bioactive compounds are present. The current D assessment therefore rests mainly on the specialist tortoise source, and an accidental small bite is not overstated as poisoning.
plants.role: Excluded from planned feeding

plants.name: Sainfoin
plants.why: A specialist tortoise plant database classifies the aerial parts of sainfoin (Onobrychis viciifolia) as feed sparingly. This is not, however, a direct trial that sets exact feeding amounts, frequency or a harmful dose. The assessment is therefore not extended to unconfirmed parts such as the roots, and only the aerial parts are used rarely and in small amounts mixed with several suitable plants. Polyphenols and condensed tannins have been analysed directly in Onobrychis viciifolia, with variation in tannin composition. The presence of tannins alone does not, however, mean toxicity in tortoises or a feeding ban. The current limited-supplement assessment is therefore kept, and the composition data for this species are added only as reference evidence.
plants.role: Limited supplement in a varied diet

plants.name: Borage
plants.why: A specialist tortoise plant database excludes borage (Borago officinalis) from planned feeding. An original paper that analysed borage leaves with precise instruments also actually detected pyrrolizidine alkaloids (PAs, plant compounds that can harm the liver) and their N-oxides. That study is not a toxicity test in tortoises, however, so it is not extended to “one bite means poisoning” or to a specific toxic dose, and the D assessment is kept.
plants.role: Excluded from planned feeding

plants.name: Henbit
plants.why: A specialist tortoise plant database classifies the aerial parts of henbit (Lamium amplexicaule) as feed sparingly. This assessment cannot automatically be applied to all other species of Lamium, and it is not a direct trial that sets an exact safe amount or feeding frequency. Only aerial parts correctly identified as L. amplexicaule are therefore used rarely and in small amounts mixed with several plants. Several secondary metabolites have been isolated and identified directly from the aerial parts of Lamium amplexicaule itself. The current limited-supplement assessment is therefore kept; the only change is that the existence of direct analyses of this species and part is reflected in the evidence certainty.
plants.role: Limited supplement in a varied diet

plants.name: House leek
plants.why: A specialist tortoise plant database classifies the new leaves and leaves of Sempervivum as feedable, but because it is a succulent, eating a lot can cause loose stools, so it should be used in moderation. This caution is not a trial that sets an exact harmful dose. New leaves and leaves are therefore used as a supplement mixed with several plants, without giving a large amount at once or repeating it as a sole ingredient.
plants.role: Supplement in a varied diet

plants.name: Echeveria
plants.why: A specialist tortoise plant database classifies the leaves, flowers and stems of Echeveria as feedable, while advising moderate use because it is a succulent. This is not, however, a trial that sets exact feeding amounts, frequency or long-term sole-feeding safety. The confirmed leaves, flowers and stems are therefore limited to a supplementary ingredient mixed with several plants, and large amounts are not fed repeatedly at one time.
plants.role: Supplement in a varied diet

plants.name: Snapdragon
plants.why: Snapdragons can be used as a supplementary plant mixed into a varied diet. A specialist tortoise plant database classifies the leaves and flowers of snapdragons (Antirrhinum spp., especially A. majus) as feedable as part of a varied diet. This is not, however, a trial that sets an exact feeding proportion or frequency or shows sole feeding is safe. Correctly identified leaves and flowers without pesticide exposure are therefore used as a supplementary ingredient mixed with several suitable plants.
plants.role: Supplement in a varied diet

plants.name: Hosta
plants.why: A specialist tortoise plant database classifies hostas (Hosta spp.) as feed in moderation, taking saponins into account. This does not mean, however, that every species, cultivar and plant part in the genus Hosta has the same composition or feeding suitability. The presence of saponins alone cannot establish a toxic dose or clinical harm in tortoises either. If the identity of the plant and the part to be fed cannot be confirmed, do not feed it; even when they are confirmed, prioritise verified foods and treat hosta only as a limited supplement.
plants.role: Limited supplement after identifying the hosta

plants.name: Salsify / Goat's beard
plants.why: A specialist tortoise plant database classifies the aerial parts of Tragopogon as feedable, but warns not to confuse it with the similarly named toxic plant Aruncus dioicus. It is not a direct trial that sets an exact feeding proportion or frequency. Only aerial parts correctly identified as Tragopogon are therefore used mixed with several suitable wild plants; if the identification is uncertain, do not feed it.
plants.role: Supplement in a varied diet

plants.name: Hawksbeard
plants.why: A specialist tortoise plant database classifies the aerial parts of Crepis as feedable. This is not, however, a direct trial that sets exact feeding amounts, frequency or long-term sole-feeding safety. Correctly identified, uncontaminated aerial parts are therefore used as a supplementary ingredient mixed with several suitable wild plants, and the assessment is not extended to unconfirmed parts such as the roots.
plants.role: Supplement in a varied diet

plants.name: Hawkbit
plants.why: A specialist tortoise plant database classifies the aerial parts of Leontodon as feedable. This is not, however, a direct trial that sets an exact feeding proportion or frequency or shows sole feeding is safe. Correctly identified aerial parts are therefore used mixed with several suitable wild plants, and the assessment is not extended to unconfirmed parts or look-alike plants.
plants.role: Supplement in a varied diet

plants.name: Cat's ear
plants.why: A specialist tortoise plant database classifies the aerial parts of cat's-ear (Hypochaeris radicata) as feedable as part of a varied diet. This is not, however, a direct trial that sets exact feeding amounts, frequency or safety as a sole staple. Correctly identified, uncontaminated aerial parts are therefore used as one ingredient of a mixed diet with several suitable wild plants.
plants.role: Supplement in a varied diet

plants.name: Hawkweed
plants.why: Hawkweeds (Hieracium) are considered only as a limited supplementary food after the exact species is confirmed. A specialist tortoise plant database considers the mature aerial parts of hawkweeds (Hieracium spp.) feedable in moderation in a varied diet. This is not, however, a direct trial that sets exact feeding amounts, frequency or long-term safety. Correctly identified mature aerial parts are therefore used in limited amounts mixed with other suitable wild plants, and this is not extended into grounds for feeding them alone or in a high proportion repeatedly.
plants.role: Limited supplement in a varied diet

plants.name: Shepherd's purse
plants.why: A specialist tortoise plant database classifies the aerial parts of shepherd's purse (Capsella bursa-pastoris) as feed in moderation because of concern about goitrogens in cabbage-family plants. This is not, however, a direct trial that quantified a harmful dose or thyroid effects of shepherd's purse in tortoises. The aerial parts are therefore used in limited amounts mixed with several plants, without letting the diet lean on cabbage-family plants.
plants.role: Limited supplement in a varied diet

plants.name: Petunia
plants.why: A specialist tortoise plant database classifies petunias (Petunia spp.) as feed in moderation. That source does not present confirmed toxicity of petunia itself, but gives conservative guidance because it belongs to the nightshade family (Solanaceae). Membership of the nightshade family alone does not make petunia toxic, nor can the petunia assessment be applied to other plants of the same family. The current evidence is not a direct trial that sets an exact safe amount or repeat-feeding frequency for tortoises. Only correctly identified petunias are treated as a limited supplement among several verified foods, and ornamental plants of unclear identity, or plants whose contamination or chemical treatment cannot be checked, are not fed.
plants.role: Limited supplement after identifying the petunia

plants.name: Dahlia
plants.why: A specialist tortoise plant database clearly separates the plant parts of dahlia: the leaves and flowers can be fed in limited amounts, but the roots and tubers should not be fed. The mild gastroenteritis and dermatitis reported in mammals cannot be assumed to appear as the same toxicity in tortoises, and this is not a direct trial that sets an exact safe amount for tortoises. Only the leaves and flowers are therefore used in small amounts mixed with several plants, and the roots and tubers are excluded from the diet.
plants.role: Supplementary plant: only leaves and flowers, mixed in limited amounts

plants.name: Gerbera
plants.why: A specialist tortoise plant database considers Gerbera usable in limited amounts as part of a varied diet and separately warns that plants from garden centres and florists may have been treated with pesticides. This is genus-level specialist information for Gerbera, not a direct trial showing that all species and cultivars are the same, nor exact feeding-amount data. Gerbera is therefore used as a small supplement among several foods only when it is correctly identified as Gerbera and new growth with no history of pesticide treatment is confirmed.
plants.role: Supplementary plant mixed occasionally into a varied diet

plants.name: Zinnia
plants.why: The leaves and flowers of zinnia can be one component of a varied mixed diet. A specialist tortoise plant database classifies the leaves and flowers of zinnias (Zinnia spp.) as feedable as part of a varied diet. This is not, however, a direct trial that sets an exact feeding proportion or frequency or shows that unlimited intake is safe. Correctly identified leaves and flowers are therefore used as a supplementary ingredient in a mixed diet.
plants.role: Leaves and flowers used as one component of a varied mixed diet of plants

plants.name: Mexican Petunia
plants.why: Correctly identified Ruellia can be used as a supplementary component of a varied mixed diet. A specialist tortoise database classifies some Ruellia spp., known in English as “Mexican petunia”, as feedable. Despite the name, it belongs to the acanthus family (Acanthaceae) and is entirely different from common petunias (nightshade family), so exact species identification matters; only confirmed Ruellia is used as part of a varied mixed diet.
plants.role: Correctly identified Ruellia used as a supplementary component of a varied mixed diet

plants.name: Coreopsis
plants.why: Coreopsis can be one component of a varied mixed diet of plants. A specialist tortoise plant database classifies Coreopsis spp. as feedable and gives no known hazards. This is not, however, a direct trial that sets an exact feeding proportion or shows that unlimited intake is safe. Correctly identified plants are therefore used as a supplementary ingredient in a varied mixed diet.
plants.role: One component of a varied mixed diet of plants

plants.name: Astilbe
plants.why: A specialist tortoise plant database classifies Astilbe as feedable. This is, however, genus-level specialist husbandry information for Astilbe; it is not a trial confirming the same safety for every species and cultivar, or direct feeding, long-term safety or exact feeding amounts in tortoises. Only plants correctly identified as Astilbe and free of contamination are therefore used as a supplementary ingredient mixed with several suitable foods.
plants.role: Supplementary component of a varied mixed diet of plants

plants.name: Primula
plants.why: A specialist tortoise plant database excludes primroses (Primula) from planned feeding. A separate original paper quantified primin, a contact skin allergen, and its precursor miconidin directly in the leaves, stems and flowers of Primula obconica, and found small amounts of primin released even from undamaged plants. This is plant-chemistry research describing contact and airborne exposure risks in people, not an oral toxicity test in tortoises. Allergen composition can also differ between Primula species and cultivars, so the P. obconica result is not applied equally to all Primula. The D is therefore kept as a conservative exclusion from planned feeding based on the specialist tortoise source, not as confirmed oral toxicity.
plants.role: Excluded from planned feeding

plants.name: Comfrey
plants.why: A specialist tortoise plant database excludes comfrey (Symphytum officinale) from planned feeding and gives pyrrolizidine alkaloids (PAs) as the key risk. An original paper actually analysed the PAs in comfrey and confirmed that exposure varies with plant part, and a separate chemical-ecology study shows that PA biosynthesis is active not only in the roots but also in certain young leaves, and that PAs can accumulate in flowers depending on the developmental stage. The types and concentrations of PAs differ with part and conditions, however, and these studies are not trials that set a toxic dose for tortoises. Claims such as “one bite causes liver damage” are therefore not made, but there is no evidence supporting the safety of repeated planned feeding, so the D assessment is kept.
plants.role: Excluded from planned feeding

plants.name: Bergamot / Bee Balm
plants.why: A specialist tortoise plant database classifies Monarda as feedable as part of a varied diet. It is called “bee balm” or “bergamot” in English, but it is an entirely different plant from Citrus bergamia, so the assessment must not be transferred on the basis of the name alone. It is also not a direct trial that sets an exact feeding proportion or frequency. Only plants correctly identified as Monarda and free of contamination are therefore used as a supplementary ingredient mixed with several foods.
plants.role: One component of a varied mixed diet of plants

plants.name: Bur clover
plants.why: When correctly identified as Medicago polymorpha, it can be used in limited amounts in a varied mixed diet of wild plants. The plant currently recorded as Medicago hispida is treated as Medicago polymorpha, and there is a record of wild Testudo graeca graeca actually eating this taxon. That wild study does not, however, establish the exact part eaten or a captive feeding proportion. A separate plant-chemistry study found saponin-type compounds in the aerial parts of this species, but it does not show from what amount they become harmful to tortoises. Without overstating “saponins = toxic”, feeding it alone or in a high proportion is avoided and it is limited to being part of a variety of wild plants.
plants.role: Component used in limited amounts in a varied mixed diet of wild plants

plants.name: Canadian horseweed
plants.why: A specialist tortoise plant database classifies Erigeron canadensis (synonym Conyza canadensis) as do not feed. A study of essential oil from the aerial parts also reported bioactivity signals, but that was a cell test with concentrated essential oil and cannot be converted into a toxic dose for tortoises eating the fresh plant. On the other hand, no direct evidence supporting safe planned feeding is currently linked either, so it is excluded from the diet.
plants.role: Excluded from planned feeding

plants.name: Butcher's broom
plants.why: Ruscus aculeatus has wild-feeding evidence but is used only in limited amounts as part of a seasonal mixed diet. There is direct observational evidence that wild Hermann's tortoises (Testudo hermanni hermanni) used the flowers and unripe fruit of Ruscus aculeatus and also ate the leaves. This is, however, a record of wild use in autumn, not a trial that sets captive feeding amounts, frequency or a long-term safe dose. Medicinal and toxicological data on root and rhizome extracts must also not be read as toxicity of the fresh leaves, flowers or unripe fruit. The aerial parts with confirmed evidence are therefore used in limited amounts as one of several plants, and the roots and rhizomes are not covered by this assessment.
plants.role: Seasonal wild plant mixed in limited amounts

plants.name: Hedge mustard
plants.why: The Tortoise Trust includes young plants of hedge mustard (Sisymbrium officinale) in its list of wild foods for tortoises, and other specialist sources classify it as feedable but not to be given in large amounts repeatedly. Plant-chemistry research has found glucosinolates and isothiocyanates. Correctly identified young plants are therefore mixed in limited amounts among several foods, and this is not extended to mature plants, seeds or to giving several other cabbage-family plants in large amounts at the same time.
plants.role: Young plants mixed in limited amounts

plants.name: Harebell
plants.why: A specialist tortoise plant database names the leaves and flowers of harebell (Campanula rotundifolia) as feedable parts and separates the rhizome as not to be fed. Correctly identified leaves and flowers can therefore be used mixed with several suitable plants. In some regions it is also called “bluebell” in English, so it must not be confused with Hyacinthoides on the basis of the name alone.
plants.role: Leaves and flowers used as part of a varied mixed diet

plants.name: Broadleaf filaree
plants.why: A specialist tortoise plant database classifies Erodium botrys as a food that can be included in a varied diet, and Kew data confirm the exact scientific name. Correctly identified plants can therefore be used as one component of a mixed diet together with several wild plants. There are, however, no trials of long-term sole feeding to tortoises or exact proportion data, so this is not extended to feeding one kind continuously like a staple.
plants.role: One component of a varied mixed diet of wild plants

plants.name: White dead-nettle
plants.why: Independent specialist tortoise sources treat Lamium album as a feedable wild plant. Correctly identified white dead-nettle can be used to add variety to the diet, mixed with several suitable wild plants. Young plants can, however, be confused with stinging nettle, so identification comes first for foraged plants, and there are no data proving long-term sole feeding or a fixed proportion.
plants.role: One component of a varied mixed diet of wild plants

plants.name: Kidney weed
plants.why: A specialist tortoise plant database classifies the genus Dichondra as feedable and gives Dichondra micrantha directly as an example. If the plant is correctly identified and has not been treated with chemicals, it can be used mixed with several suitable foods. It is, however, sometimes grown over a wide area like a lawn, as a single plant, so the assessment that it “can be eaten” is not extended into grounds for a single staple or unlimited grazing.
plants.role: Fed mixed with a variety of plant foods
plants.market: wild, grown as a lawn substitute

plants.name: Indian mallow
plants.why: Specialist tortoise sources classify the genus Abutilon as feedable and describe the flowers in particular as eaten. This is, however, genus-level guidance rather than direct feeding data on Indian mallow itself, so a conservative assessment, mixing small amounts of leaves and flowers as one of several foods, is appropriate. The same assessment is not automatically applied to the seeds or roots, and it must not be confused with the entirely different Physalis.
plants.role: Leaves and flowers mixed in small amounts to add variety

plants.name: Tree aeonium
plants.why: Aeonium arboreum is used as a succulent mixed in occasionally in small amounts, not as a staple. Specialist tortoise sources treat Aeonium as a feedable succulent, but advise mixing in only small amounts because eating a lot can soften the stools and some species can be high in calcium oxalate. Aeonium arboreum is therefore best used as a small supplementary component to add variety to the diet, not as a staple.
plants.role: Succulent mixed in occasionally in small amounts

plants.name: Butterfly bush
plants.why: A specialist tortoise plant database classifies Buddleja as feed in moderation. B. davidii, the buddleja commonly sold in Korea, belongs to the same genus, so correctly identified leaves and flowers that have not been treated with chemicals can be considered for mixing in small amounts. This is, however, genus-level husbandry guidance rather than a species-specific long-term feeding trial, so it is not grounds for feeding large amounts repeatedly like a staple.
plants.role: Mixed in occasionally in small amounts

plants.name: Common vetch
plants.why: For common vetch, only the leaves and flowers are mixed in small amounts, and the seeds and pods are excluded. With common vetch, the parts that can be eaten and the parts to avoid must be kept apart. Specialist tortoise sources consider the leaves and flowers feedable as a small part of a varied diet, but advise against feeding the pods because the seeds contain cyanogenic glycosides. Only the leaves and flowers are therefore mixed in small amounts, and once seeds or pods form, the plant is no longer fed.
plants.role: Only the leaves and flowers, mixed in small amounts
plants.market: wild, grown as forage or green manure

plants.name: Tufted vetch
plants.why: Tufted vetch is directly included in the specialist tortoise sources' Vicia entry, whose leaves and flowers can be fed as a small part of the diet. It is also used at a low proportion in some wild-plant seed mixes for tortoises. The seeds should, however, be avoided because of cyanogenic glycosides, so only the leaves and flowers are mixed in small amounts, and the pods and seeds are not given.
plants.role: Only the leaves and flowers, mixed in small amounts
